snip.t: A common language so clinicians, patients, families and services mean the same thing by "schizophrenia" or "depression".
To guide treatment: the diagnosis points to evidence-based options (for example lithium for bipolar disorder, SSRIs plus CBT for depression).
Pressured speech (mania); poverty of speech and mutism (depression, schizophrenia); slow, monotonous (depression); dysarthria or slurring (neurological, intoxication).
Seen in: Schizophrenia, mania, psychotic depression, delirium — Schizophrenia, delirium, substance use, epilepsy — Delirium, anxiety, fatigue; can be normal
Anhedonia: Loss of interest or pleasure in previously enjoyable activities; a core feature of major depression and negative symptoms.
Anergia: Lack of energy or physical drive; commonly seen in depression and negative symptom clusters.
Euthymic: Normal, stable mood without significant elevation or depression.
The monoamine hypothesis says depression involves low serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine function.

qs.q: A forensic dentist analyzes a single-rooted premolar with a root length nearly identical to the adjacent first premolar but lacking a mesial root depression. Which tooth is under review?
o: Mandibular second molar
Mandibular first premolar
Maxillary first premolar
Maxillary second premolar
Maxillary central incisor
qs.e: The maxillary second premolar typically has a single root that lacks the prominent mesial root depression found on the first premolar.

qs.q: An anatomical study examines a normal adult heart and identifies the fossa ovalis. The elevated rim surrounding this depression represents the persistent free edge of which embryonic structure?
o: Muscular fold known as the septum secundum
Resorbed superior margin of septum primum
Fused portion of left and right venous valves
Remnant of obliterated ductus arteriosus wall
Proximal margin of dorsal mesocardium fold
qs.e: The limbus fossa ovalis is formed by the distinct lower free edge of the developing septum secundum.

qs.q: A patient with diabetes mellitus has a serum osmolality of 320 mOsm/kg. The laboratory uses a freezing point depression method to measure osmolality. What is the primary principle behind this technique?
o: Light refraction measurement through the solution.
Boiling point elevation proportional to solute concentration.
Electrical conductivity measurement of the solution.
Freezing point depression proportional to solute concentration.
Vapor pressure measurement of the solution.
qs.e: Freezing point depression is directly proportional to the total concentration of osmotically active particles in the solution.

qs.q: A patient with depression is prescribed an SSRI. After two weeks, they report no improvement. Which mechanism best explains why SSRIs often require several weeks to show therapeutic effects?
o: The drug takes time to reach therapeutic concentrations in brain tissue
The drug must first deplete the existing serotonin stores in the neuron
The drug needs time to increase the production of new serotonin molecules
The drug requires time to downregulate serotonin receptors for homeostasis
The drug requires time to cross the blood-brain barrier in quantities
qs.e: SSRIs require time for receptor downregulation and neuroplastic changes to produce therapeutic effects.

qs.q: A patient with depression is prescribed an MAOI. They are told to avoid tyramine-rich foods. Which mechanism best explains this dietary restriction?
o: Tyramine raises cortisol levels, which could lead to adrenal insufficiency.
Tyramine blocks serotonin reuptake, possibly causing serotonin syndrome.
Tyramine inhibits dopamine action, potentially producing extrapyramidal symptoms.
Tyramine increases GABA activity, leading to excessive sedation.
Tyramine is a sympathomimetic amine that can provoke a hypertensive crisis when combined with MAOIs.
qs.e: Tyramine can cause a hypertensive crisis when combined with MAOIs due to its sympathomimetic properties.

qs.q: A 28-year-old man is brought in with severe respiratory depression and profound sedation after taking diazepam concurrently with another substance. Which combination is most notorious for causing fatal respiratory depression?
o: Diazepam combined with central nervous system depressants
Diazepam combined with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Diazepam combined with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
Diazepam combined with high doses of water-soluble vitamins
Diazepam combined with broad-spectrum bacteriostatic agents
qs.e: Co-administration of diazepam with alcohol or opioids produces synergistic central nervous system and respiratory depression.

qs.q: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus develops new-onset psychosis and depression. Which autoantibody has a strongly established odds ratio for these specific psychiatric manifestations?
o: Anti-centromere antibody
Anti-SCL-70 antibody
Anti-ribosomal-P antibody
Anti-JO-1 antibody
qs.e: Anti-ribosomal-P antibodies carry a 4 to 10 times odds ratio for psychosis and depression in SLE patients. Other antibodies like anti-SCL-70 are typically associated with scleroderma rather than lupus-related psychiatric symptoms.

qs.q: A psychiatric patient with major depression is prescribed fluoxetine. What is the primary mechanism of action of this first-line antidepressant class?
o: Blockade of serotonin reuptake transporter mechanisms
Blockade of both norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake
Enhancement of GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening
Inhibition of monoamine oxidase enzyme activity
qs.e: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like fluoxetine act by blocking the reuptake of serotonin. Tricyclic antidepressants block both NE and serotonin reuptake, while MAOIs inhibit monoamine oxidase.

ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Depression is a common mood disorder marked by persistent low mood, loss of interest, and functional impairment. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria and severity grading.

b: Prevalence ~5% worldwide, higher in low‑resource settings
Higher risk with chronic illness, trauma, and social adversity
sections.p: Depression affects thoughts, emotions, and physical health. It can be episodic or chronic and is diagnosed when symptoms persist for at least two weeks.

b: Severity: mild (1‑2 functional domains impaired), moderate (3‑4), severe (≥5 or psychosis)
Typical symptoms: sleep change, appetite change, fatigue, guilt, concentration difficulty, suicidality
sections.p: Use DSM‑5/ICD‑10 criteria: ≥5 symptoms, one must be depressed mood or anhedonia, lasting ≥2 weeks, causing distress or impairment.

t.b: Quantifies symptom burden; score ≥10 suggests moderate depression, ≥20 severe
Structured diagnostic interview; confirms DSM‑5 criteria when clinician time limited

b: Screen all patients with chronic illness, pregnancy, or recent loss
Consider secondary causes: hypothyroidism, anemia, HIV, post‑infectious states
sections.p: Depression worsens outcomes of HIV, TB, malaria, and chronic diseases; it increases mortality via suicide and poor self‑care.

t.b: Rule out hypothyroidism mimicking depression; low TSH = hyperthyroidism, high TSH = hypothyroidism
Detect anemia or iron deficiency, common in low‑resource settings and can present with fatigue

b: Ask directly about thoughts of self‑harm
Distinguish grief (normal timeline) from depressive disorder
sections.p: Focus on symptom count, duration, functional impact, and safety. Always assess suicidality.

b: Assuming low mood after loss is always depression
Prescribing antidepressants without checking for drug interactions (e.g., MAO inhibitors, HIV meds)
sections.p: Avoid over‑reliance on single lab values; depression is clinical. Do not miss medical mimics or treat only with medication without psychosocial support.

whenToSeekHelp: Suicidal ideation with plan or intent
Rapid worsening of function or inability to care for basic needs
